name: Dusty rose brown
lede: Dusty rose brown is a muted, greyed pink-brown recorded by Werner in 1821, its name a plain description with no further story behind the choice of words.

sections.title: A muted rose
sections.body:
Our library traces this color to Werner's 1821 nomenclature, which ties its near-duplicate, a shade it calls Brownish Purple Red, to a natural example: the flower of deadly nightshade [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[crocus-martis]], [[rose-castor]], [[reddish-grey]] and [[fontainebleau]], at 2.9, 3.2, 
In ISCC-NBS terms it reads as a light grayish reddish brown, in Munsell notation 8.8R 5.0/2.2 [1]. Close lookalikes in our library include [[crocus-martis]] and [[rose-castor]], both almost the same hue [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this muted pink-brown in 240 of 23,781 paintings, 1.01 percent, more common than 63 percent of our named colors, as photographed [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 42 of 1,674 paintings, nearly four times the archive's baseline rate for that century, and most often hides in shadow, in 46 percent of its appearances [2]. Félix Vallotton favors it most, in 5 of his 40 catalogued works, over six times the baseline for the museums those works come from [2]. The earliest dated example, from 1340, predates Werner's 1821 record of the name by nearly five centuries, so the match is a look-alike hue in aged paint, not proof of the pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

choices: A desaturated, muted version of rose-brown
